title: Wetlands: Nature's Kidneys

endcard.line: Footage: BLM Oregon & Washington (public domain). Pictures: Sankara Subramanian (CC BY 2.0); Government of Odisha (CC BY 4.0)

segments.say: A marsh can look like wasted land. It is actually doing three jobs at once.
First, it cleans water. Plants slow the flow, mud settles out, and the water that moves on is cleaner. That is why wetlands are called nature's kidneys.

anim.title: Job two: a sponge
items: Keeps streams flowing in dry months

segments.say: Second, it works like a sponge. It soaks up floodwater and releases it slowly, which lowers floods downstream and keeps streams flowing in the dry season.
In the United States, wetlands along the Mississippi once stored at least sixty days of floodwater.
Third, it is home. Fish breed in it, and birds like these painted storks at Keoladeo in Rajasthan come to feed.
Keoladeo and Chilika lake in Odisha were India's first two Ramsar sites, in nineteen eighty-one. The Ramsar treaty itself was signed in Iran in nineteen seventy-one.
For Prelims: wetlands filter water, store floods and shelter life. The treaty is Ramsar, nineteen seventy-one.

sources: US EPA, 'Why are Wetlands Important?': wetlands protect and improve water quality, act as natural sponges that trap and slowly release floodwater, maintain surface flow in dry periods, provide fish and wildlife habitat; Mississippi bottomland wetlands once stored at least 60 days of floodwater
Wikipedia, 'Ramsar Convention': signed at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 (World Wetlands Day)
Wikipedia, 'List of Ramsar sites in India': Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park were India's first sites, 1 October 1981

quiz.q: Why are wetlands called nature's kidneys?
quiz.why: Plants slow the flow and mud settles out, so the water moving on is cleaner.

quiz.q: Where was the Ramsar Convention signed?
Which two were India's first Ramsar sites?
quiz.why: Chilika and Keoladeo joined the list in 1981.

reviewNote: Facts were read against US EPA's wetlands page and summary pages for the Ramsar Convention and India's Ramsar list; check the 1981 date on the Ramsar Sites Information Service before approval. 'Nature's kidneys' is a common nickname, not an official term. Video 233 (Ramsar sites) covers the list itself, so this one stays on what wetlands do. Moving facts: India's Ramsar count changes often, so no count is given.
